newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish market rates seen flat after reserve rise.
newsitem.headline: Polish market rates seen flat after reserve rise.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland's increase in mandatory reserves from the end of February will not have a large impact on market rates but its effect on client credit and deposit rates was still hazy, analysts said.
Analysts said banks would likely curb roll-over investments in the NBP's drainages next month to offset lower liquidity resulting from the obligatory reserves rise.
"The drop in liquidity will not be significant enough to cause market rates to rise, as demand for NBP-bills may fall in March," said Andrzej Hirsz, senior dealer at Bank Gdanski SA .
Analysts said 1.6 billion zlotys worth of NBP-bills mature in March against the estimated liquidity loss of 1.3 billion coming from the central bank's reserves increase.

Some said however, that money market rates may rise 0.5 point above the main central bank reverse repo rate of 21.64 percent in the second half of February when banks look for funds to compensate larger outflows from the start of March.
"I expect a modest rise of 0.5 point later this month," said Radoslaw Radziszewski, deputy chief dealer at Pekao SA.

Late last month the central bank announced that from February 28 it was increasing mandatory reserves on zloty call deposits to 20 percent from the current 17 percent and was doubling the reserves on currency deposits to four percent.

The move came after the NBP had signalled it was concerned with fast credit expansion and was considering a rise in its official lombard and discount rates, now at 25 and 22 percent respectively, or other measures, to control money supply.

Central bank head Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said that real interest rates would grow but that future decisions on official rates, now at 25 and 22 percent, would depend on the impact the increase of obligatory reserves.

"We have to see what will be the behaviour of banks after the increase of reserve requirements, what will be the impact of the increased requirements on market interest rates, reverse repos and others," she said earlier this week.
Analysts said they were watching credit and deposit rate changes at Poland's biggest retailer, state-owned savings bank PKO BP, to set the tone for the rest of the banking sector.
